claims.text: FeCoNiCrAl deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock has insufficient bond-coat thickness for the intended TBC application.
Changing the FeCoNiCrAl feedstock size from 15–45 μm to 60–90 μm will produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness.
The larger feedstock will produce a bond coat that meets the required thickness.
The larger-feedstock coating will retain similar or improved coating integrity relative to the 15–45 μm baseline.
The larger-feedstock coating will have only a minimal increase in as-sprayed oxidation relative to the baseline.
Larger feedstock particles produce relatively larger molten droplets during flight.
Larger droplets have a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio.
The lower surface-area-to-volume ratio of larger droplets reduces in-flight oxidation.
Larger particles have higher kinetic energy upon impact.
Higher impact kinetic energy improves droplet flattening and coating adhesion.
Increasing particle size increases the deposited mass per particle impact.
Larger particles melt more completely under the proposed thermal-spray conditions.
The larger feedstock increases deposition efficiency.
Higher deposition efficiency produces a thicker and denser coating without compromising integrity or oxidation state.
An inert or well-shielded argon atmosphere controls oxidation during deposition.
The thickness benefit depends on adjusting spray distance, power, and carrier-gas flow for the larger particles.
Excessively increasing particle size without process optimization can cause poor flattening or weak bonding.
Higher inertia of larger droplets can cause splashing.
Inadequate melting of larger particles can prevent the predicted deposition benefit.
The larger-feedstock benefit will remain effective during high-temperature cyclic exposure in air representative of TBC service.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that spray distance, power, and carrier-gas flow must be tuned for larger particles, but the proposed controlled experiment holds all spraying parameters identical except feedstock size. Thus, the experiment does not test the intervention under the conditions asserted to be necessary for its success.

The mechanism states categorically that larger particles melt more completely, whereas the boundary explicitly identifies inadequate melting of larger particles as a possible reason the benefit may fail. This is unresolved because no parameter regime is specified in which complete melting is expected.
